podcast-joerogan-Fn_bfhvoX2c:
A woman named Suzanne and her spiritual acid trip anchor a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Rogan retells her experience as a story about what a single strong trip can do to a person's outlook. The show collects tales like this the way other shows collect news clips.

The account follows the trip's arc, from the dose to the sense of unity that gave the story its name. Rogan adds his own view of why such nights stick with people for years. The segment is a short, warm trip report, less about the drug than about the meaning a person brings home from it.
uslaw-usc-t2-s142c:
Section 142c of Title 2 of the United States Code covers enforcement of the liability of certifying officers of the Library of Congress. It sits in Chapter 5 of Title 2, on the Library, current through Public Law 119-134. The text shown is the closing part of the provision.

That liability is to be enforced in the same manner and to the same extent as the law provides for disbursing and other accountable officers. The certifying officers hold a right of their own under the section. They may apply for, and obtain, a decision by the Comptroller General. That decision may be sought on any question of law involved in a payment on any vouchers put to them for certification. The rule thus pairs their exposure with a route to an advance ruling on doubtful points of law.
uslaw-usc-t2-s182c:
Section 182c of Title 2 of the United States Code sets up a revolving fund for two Library of Congress programs. It sits in Chapter 5 of Title 2, on the Library of Congress, current through Public Law 119-134. The programs are the Federal Library and Information Network program, called the FEDLINK program, and the Federal Research program.

A separate account must be kept in the revolving fund for each of the two programs. The Librarian may charge a fee for services under either program. Fees charged are paid into the account of the revolving fund for the program that earned them. Participants in the programs pay for products and services under the advance-of-funds rules the section goes on to state.
uslaw-usc-t2-s282c:
Section 282c of Title 2 of the United States Code covers expenditures by the House Office of Legislative Counsel. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on that office, in the House administration part. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. The office drafts bill language for House members.

In accord with policies and procedures approved by the Speaker, the Counsel may spend funds, the text states. Spending must be such as is needed or fitting for the functioning of the office. Speaker approved policy is the control on that spending power. A drafting office that must stay neutral thus buys its supplies under the Speaker's framework, not its own whim.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2c:
Section 2c of Title 2 of the United States Code requires states to draw single-member districts for the House of Representatives. It applies to any state entitled to more than one Representative. The entitlement flows from an apportionment made under section 2a of the same title.

In such a state, a number of districts equal to its number of Representatives must be established by law. Representatives are then elected only from the districts so established. No district may elect more than one Representative, apart from an exception the text begins to state. The rule applies from the Ninety-first Congress onward, and to every Congress after it. The section is the statutory root of the modern district map: one district, one member, drawn by state law.
